hero.title: What does a dollar really cost?
hero.body: In much of the world the official exchange rate is not the rate anyone gets. This measures what people actually pay for a dollar — the kind an ordinary person can buy on their phone — in {count} currencies, every hour. Where there is no price, it says so, and why.

board.title: What a dollar really costs
board.subhead: measured every hour · furthest above the official rate first
board.withheldNote: A price was collected for these and stored, but it does not meet the evidence rule, so it is not shown as a number. Each country keeps its page and its reason, and returns as soon as its market does.
board.footnote: Each row is one country. "A dollar costs" is what you pay to buy one dollar there, against the official exchange rate captured in the same second. "Round trip" is what it costs to buy and then sell again. Click any country for every source behind its number.
board.gapsNote: The eight countries where a dollar costs the most above the official rate.
board.pricedNote: Each one links to its own page, with the full history and the receipt behind the number.

cross.title: If you moved money through the dollar route, what rate would you get?
cross.intro: Turn {baseCode} into a digital dollar on a {baseCountry} exchange, then turn that dollar into the other country's money on an exchange there. This is the rate that round trip works out to, next to the official rate for the same moment.
cross.footnote: A plus means the dollar route works out to more of the other country's money than the official rate would give you, before any fees.

corridor.title: Is it a real dollar?
corridor.lede1: Every price on this site is the price of a digital dollar — the kind an ordinary person can buy on their phone, in places where the bank won't sell them one. So the obvious question is whether that's a real dollar or just a number on a screen.
corridor.lede2: We answer it the only honest way: we take one all the way through. Buy it in one country, move it, sell it in another, pay every fee on the way. Then we count what actually came out the other end.
corridor.verdict1: Doing this is almost always more expensive than just using a bank. We've measured it {measureCount} times. The stablecoin route came out cheaper {winCount} times.
corridor.verdict2: We publish that because the point was never to sell you on it. The round trip isn't advice, it's a test: if the digital dollar weren't a real dollar, the money wouldn't come out the other end at all. It does, minus a cost we can show you line by line.

landed.title: What came out the other end
landed.cap: The landed amount, against what a bank would have given you for the same transfer, right now.

waterfall.title: Where the money goes
waterfall.cap: Three things happen to your money: you buy the coin, you move it, you sell it. Each bar is what that step costs at this amount. Bars left of the line are money you gain, right of the line are money you lose. The dashed line is the cheapest ordinary provider, same second.

ladder.title: It is worst at the amounts people actually send
ladder.capTemplate: The blockchain charges the same flat fee whatever you send, so it barely registers on a large transfer and dominates a small one. {highlight} is highlighted.

history.title: Every round trip we've run
history.cap: The total cost over time, hourly since collection began: buying at the price on offer, waiting for your own price, and the cheapest ordinary provider. History cannot be back-filled.

corridor.footerTemplate: The coin is bought on {onrampVenue} in {srcCcy} and sold on {offrampVenue} for {dst}. The comparison is the Wise comparison API — advertised retail prices, not confirmed fills, and they can carry promotional pricing (first-transfer or new-customer offers) recorded exactly as quoted. The comparison is therefore the best advertised price at that instant, not necessarily the best recurring one. Official exchange rates: open.er-api.com. "Waiting for your own price" assumes the order fills at the top of the book. Pricing that large institutions get privately is invisible by nature and never estimated.
